family.question: What is the person here to do?

options.browse: Look through a set of similar things: results, a catalogue, a feed, an inbox, a directory, records.
options.monitor: See numbers and status at a glance: usage, health, progress, balances, today's summary.
options.inspect: Understand one thing in depth: a product, a place, a person, an order, an event, an article.
options.act: Commit to or confirm one action, or review something just before or just after it happens.
options.input: Provide or change information: fill in details, adjust settings, answer questions.
options.follow: Do something step by step: a how-to, a recipe, a checklist, troubleshooting.

stakes.question: If this goes wrong, how bad is it for the person?
levels: Nothing is at stake; the person is only looking.
A small inconvenience that is easy to undo.
Money, time, or data is involved; undoing it takes effort.
Irreversible: a deletion, a payment, a commitment that cannot be taken back.

urgency.question: How quickly does the person need to act on what they see?
levels: No hurry; they are browsing or reading.
Soon; something is due or pending.
Right now; something is failing, expiring, or happening.

archetypes.criteria: A collection to look through, where the items matter more than any one of them.
A few options the person is weighing against each other, with the same attributes for each.
Numbers and status at a glance, with the most important figure first.
One thing in depth: what it is, its key figures, its description, its particulars, what it contains, what can be done with it.
The outcome of something the person just did: success, failure, a receipt, nothing found.
One short decision about one thing, asked before it happens: confirm, delete, approve, allow.
Review and commit: a cart, an order or booking summary with totals, a payment.
Data entry: creating or editing a record, a booking, a survey, a request with several fields.
Preferences, account options, or configuration, arranged as groups of rows that each hold one setting.
Instructions followed in order: a how-to, a method, troubleshooting, an onboarding checklist.
Something to read: an explanation, a story, a report, documentation, where the text is the point.
What happened, in order: shipment events, an audit trail, a build's stages, a patient's history, a project's milestones.
A place, or something at a place: where it is, how to get there, what is nearby.
A conversation: messages between people or with an assistant, in order, each with who said it and when.

gate.question: Does something here need the person's attention before anything else?
gate.yes: A warning, an outage, a deadline, an error, an offer about to expire, or a success to acknowledge.
gate.no: Nothing unusual is going on; this is business as usual.

tone.question: For the person looking at this, what kind of news is {title}?

options.success: Good news or a healthy state: done, available, on time, paid, active.
options.warning: Needs attention soon: low, delayed, pending, degraded, expiring.
options.danger: Bad news: failed, overdue, critical, cancelled, offline.
options.neutral: Plain information that is neither good nor bad.

gate.question: Should a picture lead this?
gate.yes: One visual subject leads: a place, dish, product, property, animal, trip, event, person, or artwork.
gate.no: The subject has no look: an order, an account, a transaction, a setting, a set of figures.

framing.question: What kind of picture is this, and how should it be framed?

options.banner: A wide scene that can be cropped: a place, a landscape, a venue, a dish on a table, a product in use.
options.portrait: A person or a face: shown whole, square or round, never cropped at the head.
options.object: A thing on its own that must not be cropped: a product on a plain background, a logo, a diagram, a chart image.
options.poster: Taller than wide and read whole: a book cover, a poster, a document page, a phone screenshot.

prominence.question: How much of the screen should this picture take?
levels: A small mark beside the title: a logo or avatar.
A supporting picture beside the text, about a third of the width.
A leading picture across the full width above the text.
The picture is the content; everything else is a caption.

gate.question: Will the person need to search or narrow down what is shown?
gate.yes: There are many items, more than fit on a screen, in recognisable categories.
gate.no: There are only a few items, or nothing to narrow.

categories.note: the distinct values of an enum field across the items, or a sibling list of category names; how they are drawn is the catalog's choice

gate.question: Are there a few values the person wants at a glance before anything else?
gate.yes: Key figures or states such as totals, counts, rates, balances, scores, durations, a status, a next time, on or off.
gate.no: The values are details to look up, not headlines, or there are too many for any to stand out.

salience.question: How important is {label} to the person at a glance?
levels: A detail they might look up.
One of the main things they came to see.
The single most important value here.

deltas.question: Do these values change over time in a way the person tracks?
deltas.yes: Usage, spending, revenue, health, or performance compared with a previous period or a target.
deltas.no: Fixed figures such as counts or specifications, with nothing to compare against.

gauge.question: Is {label} read as a level between empty and full?
gauge.yes: Progress, capacity, battery, utilization, a score out of a maximum.
gauge.no: A plain number that happens to have bounds.

news.question: For the person looking at this, is the change in {label} good or bad news?

options.good: The figure moved the way the person wants it to.
options.bad: The figure moved the way the person does not want.
options.neutral: Neither; it is just a change.

state_tone.question: Is {label} being {value} good, bad, or neutral for the person?

options.success: Good: active, healthy, on, done, in stock.

gate.question: Is there something to play here?
gate.yes: A video, an episode, a recording, a song, a voice note.
gate.no: The link is to a file or page, not something played in place.

gate.question: Is there a series of values over time or categories that is easier to read as a chart than as numbers?
gate.yes: A trend, a history, a breakdown by category, a comparison of several series.
gate.no: Single figures, or a list of records that are not a series.

gate.question: Are there particulars the person would look up, such as a reference, a date, an address, a status, a total?
gate.yes: Labelled values that are read, not acted on: order number, date, address, status, total, owner.
gate.no: There are no such particulars, or they are already shown as headline figures.

gate.question: Is there something to read, a sentence or more, that explains or describes?
gate.yes: A description, a summary, an explanation, a message, terms, a note.
gate.no: Only short labels and values; nothing to read in sentences.

length.note: Computed, never asked. Patterns may vary by it (an article gets a heading and may be collapsed behind a Read more where the catalog can; a line is set inline). The rules use it too: article-length prose moves to the front of detail and suppresses the picture's prominence to supporting.

gate.question: Are there several similar items the person would scan or pick from?
gate.yes: Results, products, people, records, messages, line items, episodes, devices, or any set of comparable things.
gate.no: This is about one thing, or the list is only a series of numbers.

layout.question: How should these items be laid out?

options.rows: Dense rows to scan quickly: text matters more than pictures, or there are many items.
options.cards: Large picture cards, one per row: the person chooses mostly by look among a few rich items.
options.grid: A grid of small picture tiles: many visual items browsed casually.
options.reel: A sideways-scrolling shelf of picture cards: a short set of suggestions or a gallery.

layout.note: pattern:<name>.<variant> means the option is offered only when the catalog's pattern has that variant, so a catalog that would draw grid as a reel is not asked about grid.

leading.question: What should lead each item, so the person knows what kind of thing it is?

options.thumbnail: A small picture of the item.
options.icon: A symbol for the item's kind or state.

options.chevron: A way in: tapping the item opens it.
options.button: One action on each item, such as Book, Add, Play.
options.value: A figure or status read at a glance.

badge_tone.question: Is {badge} good, bad, or neutral news for the person?

options.success: Good: active, done, in stock, on time.

gate.question: Is the person choosing among these few options by comparing the same attributes?
gate.yes: Plans, flights, products, candidates, quotes: a handful of options with price, time, or features side by side.
gate.no: They are not alternatives to each other, or there are too many to compare side by side.

headline_attribute.question: Which attribute will the person decide on first?

gate.question: Are these things done in order, one after another?
gate.yes: Instructions, a method, a checklist, stages of a process, a timeline of what happened.
gate.no: They are independent items with no order to follow.

gate.question: Does the person need to type or choose values here?
gate.yes: Details to fill in: name, date, amount, notes, a choice among options.
gate.no: Everything is read-only, or the only choice is a button.

options.shortText: A word or a line: a name, a title, a code.
options.longText: Several lines: notes, a message, a description.
options.number: A quantity or amount typed as digits.
options.obscured: A secret: a password or PIN.
options.toggle: On or off, and it takes effect at once.
options.choice: One of a few named options.
options.range: A value between a minimum and a maximum, where the exact number matters less than the position.
options.date: A date, a time, or both.

required.question: Must {label} be filled in before this can be submitted?
required.yes: The task cannot proceed without it.
required.no: It is optional or has a sensible default.

gate.question: Are these settings, each one a row the person can read and change?
gate.yes: Preferences and options grouped by topic: notifications, privacy, playback, account.
gate.no: This is a single form to fill in and submit, not a set of standing preferences.

options.switch: One setting that is on or off and takes effect at once.
options.value: A setting whose current value is shown and opens a picker of options when tapped.
options.navigation: A way into another page of settings or information.
options.danger: An action that removes or disconnects something: sign out, delete account.

gate.question: Is there something the person would do next from here, with a button?
gate.yes: Buy, book, save, send, confirm, retry, open, share.
gate.no: Nothing to do; the person only reads this.

primary.question: Which of these is the one thing the person most likely came to do?

destructive.question: Does {label} remove, cancel, or spend something that cannot be easily undone?
destructive.yes: Delete, cancel, sign out, pay, send.
destructive.no: It opens, saves, continues, or can be undone.

gate.question: Are these events that happened at particular times, best read in order?
gate.yes: Shipment scans, an audit log, build stages, visits, milestones, messages in a thread.
gate.no: The times are incidental; the items are things, not events.

order.question: Which end does the person want first?

options.latest: The most recent event matters most: tracking, a log, a feed of updates.
options.earliest: The sequence is read from the start: a history, a story, a plan.

state_tone.question: Is {title} ({state}) good, bad, or neutral news?

gate.question: Does the person need to see where this is?
gate.yes: A place to go to, something nearby, a route, an area.
gate.no: The address is a fact to read, as on a receipt or a profile.

gate.question: Is this a back-and-forth between people, or between a person and an assistant?
gate.yes: Messages, replies, a chat log, a support thread, comments in order.
gate.no: A list of records that happen to have an author, such as articles or reviews.

self.question: Which author is the person reading this?
self.note: Decides which side messages sit on; none means a transcript with every message on the left.

gate.question: Can the person reply or add to this here?
gate.yes: An open conversation, a comment thread they take part in, a form of one field and a send button.
gate.no: A closed transcript or a log they only read.

gate.question: Is this telling the person how something they did turned out?
gate.yes: Order placed, payment failed, message sent, nothing found, account deleted.
gate.no: Nothing has just happened; this is information or a task in progress.

tone.question: Did {headline} go well for the person?

options.neutral: Partly, or it is still pending.

rules.rule: A block marked ! is present whatever its gate says; its gate is still asked so the trace can show disagreement.
If fewer than atLeast blocks pass, include the highest-probability expected blocks until the count is met, before considering the archetype ineligible.
At most one button in actions is primary. If stakes >= 2 and a button is destructive, the destructive button is never primary and the non-destructive way out is placed first.

actions, filters, form, groups, compose, and collection.trailing=button require actions_allowed, which is archetype confidence >= gate, where gate runs linearly from 0.70 at stakes 0 to 0.95 at stakes 3: gate = 0.70 + 0.25 * stakes / 3. Low-stakes toggles need 0.70; a payment needs 0.95. The floor and cap are grammar thresholds (actionGateFloor, actionGateCap) so a deployment can tighten them.

An archetype is offered only if every required block resolves to a pattern on the surface's catalogs after walking its fallback chain. Eligibility is computed once per catalog set and cached; ineligible archetypes cost nothing at query time.

A pointer bound to a slot in one block is not offered to later blocks in the same region, except key-derived labels. Blocks claim pointers in archetype order, so a status shown in a banner is not repeated as a headline tile.
picture, collection.layout in {cards, grid, reel}, and comparison.picture are only offered when an image_url pointer exists; the anatomy question is still asked so the answer can be traced.
Every item in a collection has the same leading kind; if the picture slot is bound for fewer than half the items, leading falls back to icon or none.
If urgency >= 1.5, prose is dropped unless required, headline tiles are limited to 3, and the primary action is placed in the frame's sticky slot when the catalog's page pattern supports it.
A block whose required slots cannot be bound is dropped; an archetype whose required block is dropped is ineligible.
Every block's fallback chain entries must be abstract pattern names or pattern:variant forms such as collection:cards; the loader rejects a grammar with unknown fallback entries.

lint: Every archetype has at least one required or expected block.
Every block id used in an archetype exists in blocks.
Every fallback entry is an abstract pattern name or a pattern:variant form.
Every {placeholder} in a question names a field or slot of that block.
Every requires entry names a slot, a knob option, or a known capability flag.
